title: Westmark growth (fictional) misses, but last quarter is revised up
setup: Fictional Westmark publishes its quarterly [[gdp|GDP]] estimate. The headline growth figure is below the consensus, but the same report revises the previous quarter up from 0.6% to 0.9%. Inflation is above the central bank's target. All figures are made up; this is a practice scenario, not a forecast.
pricedIn: Moderate. Recent jobs data had been strong and traders expected solid growth. Their bets implied rates staying high for some time. Over the two quarters together, growth of 0.9% then 0.2% is about the same as the 0.6% then 0.5% expected before the revision.
question: Growth comes in at 0.2% against a 0.5% consensus, a −0.3-point surprise, while the previous quarter is revised up by 0.3 points. Which reactions are plausible?

reactions.text: WMK dips on the headline miss, then recovers as traders notice the revision.
reactions.explanation: Plausible: fast reactions often follow the headline; slower ones take in the whole report.

reactions.text: WMK falls and stays lower as traders expect rates to be cut sooner.
reactions.explanation: Plausible: if traders focus on the latest quarter's slowdown, rate expectations can shift down.

reactions.text: Little net change, since growth over two quarters is about as expected.
reactions.explanation: Plausible: the miss and the revision roughly cancel out over the two quarters.

reactions.text: WMK must fall sharply, because revisions never matter to markets.
reactions.explanation: Not plausible: revisions change the picture of the economy and can matter a lot.

takeaway: A headline miss is not the whole story. Read revisions and the full report, and remember that growth is read alongside jobs and inflation.
